question: The Edison SpA project for a coastal LNG depot in the port of Brindisi was authorised by Ministerial Decree No 17487 of 22 August 2022 without undergoing an environmental impact assessment (EIA).

The Region of Puglia had approved the project subject to the adoption of technical solutions to enable boil-off gas (BOG) to be fed into the network via a bidirectional connection to methane pipelines, a requirement accepted by Edison and incorporated into the project. This configuration would appear to qualify the depot as a regasification terminal connected to the network.

It should thus be subject to an EIA under the national legislation transposing the relevant EU Directive, as confirmed by a ministerial opinion issued in 2023 on a similar plant in the port of Oristano.

Moreover, the Brindisi depot is located in an area with establishments – that already exist or are in the process of being authorised – that are classified as major accident risks, yet there has been no assessment of the domino effects in accordance with Directive 2012/18/EU. In view of the above, I would ask the Commission: 1.

Is the authorisation issued by the Italian State, in the absence of a prior EIA, compatible with the EU legislation on environmental assessment for projects that constitute regasification terminals because of their connection to the grid?
Does the failure to examine the domino effects linked to the presence, in the same area, of other plants at risk of major accidents constitute a breach of Directive 2012/18/EU?
answer: EN on behalf of the European Commission (1.6.2026) The construction of a coastal Liquefied Natural Gas depot in the port of Brindisi by Edison SpA may fall within the scope of Annex II, point 3(c) (Surface storage of natural gas) of the Environmental Impact Assessment (EIA) Directive1.

Under Article 4(2) of the Directive, ’for projects listed in Annex II, Member States shall determine whether the project shall be made subject to an assessment in accordance with Articles 5 to 10 […]’. The Seveso III Directive2 applies to establishments where dangerous substances may be present in quantities exceeding certain thresholds, thereby qualifying for upper or lower-tier requirements.
Member States are required to ensure that operators of such establishments take all necessary measures to prevent major accidents and limit their consequences for human health and the environment.

In addition, under Article 9 of the Directive, Member States must identify all Seveso establishments or groups of establishments where the risk or consequences of a major accident may be increased due to potential domino effects.

Based on the information available, the Commission cannot confirm whether the authorisation issued by the Italian authorities is compatible with the EIA and Seveso III Directives nor whether a prior EIA was required for the project at stake.

National authorities are primarily responsible to ensure compliance with the above EU legislation, particularly the competent national administrative and/or judicial authorities. Without prejudice to its role as guardian of the Treaty, the Commission’s enforcement action regarding bad implementation of EU law focuses mainly on systemic failures3 rather than on individual projects.
1 Directive 2011/92/EU of the European Parliament and of the Council of 13 December 2011 on the assessment

of the effects of certain public and private projects on the environment (codification), OJ L 26, 28.1.2012, p. 1– 21, as amended by Directive 2014/52/EU of the European Parliament and of the Council of 16 April 2014 amending Directive 2011/92/EU on the assessment of the effects of certain public and private projects on the environment, OJ L 124, 25.4.2014, p. 1–18.

2 Directive 2012/18/EU of the European Parliament and of the Council of 4 July 2012 on the control of majoraccident hazards involving dangerous substances, amending and subsequently repealing Council Directive 96/82/EC, OJ L 197, 24.7.2012, pp. 1–37. 3 Communication from the Commission, EU law: Better results through better application, C/2016/8600, OJ C 18, 19.1.2017, p.
10–20; Communication from the Commission, Enforcing EU law for a Europe that delivers, COM(2022) 518 final, 13.10.2022.
